ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, a slider that can be regarded as a particle slides down from rest from point A at height H＝12 m along the smooth track AB, enters a vertical circular ring of radius r＝4 m, and the coefficient of kinetic friction between the track in the circular ring and the slider is the same everywhere. When the slider reaches the top point C of the circular ring, the pressure of the slider on the track is exactly zero. The slider continues to slide down along CFB, enters the smooth track BD, and when it reaches point D at height h, its speed is zero. Then the possible value of h is (magnitude of gravitational acceleration $g=10 \mathrm{m/s^{2}}$)(　　)

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the figure, a slider that can be regarded as a particle slides down from rest from point A at height H=12 m along the smooth track AB, enters a vertical circular ring of radius r=4 m, and the coefficient of kinetic friction between the track in the circular ring and the slider is the same everywhere. When the slider reaches the top point C of the circular ring, the pressure of the slider on the track is exactly zero. The slider continues to slide down along CFB, enters the smooth track BD, and when it reaches point D at height h, its speed is zero. Given that the magnitude of gravitational acceleration is g=10 m/s^2, find what the possible value of h may be?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, the dashed horizontal line serves as the height reference; the lowest point of the circular ring is marked as B, and B is on the dashed reference line; the highest point of the circular ring is C, and the radius is r, so the height of C relative to B is 2r. The smooth track on the left slides down from point A to point B, and the height of point A is marked as H; after the slider enters the vertical circular ring, it rises along the right side through E to C, then returns to B along the left side through F; afterward it rises along the smooth track on the right to point D, and the height of point D is marked as h. In the figure, the height H at A and the height h at D both take the dashed reference as zero height. Reasoning: AB and BD are smooth, and only inside the circular ring is there friction. It is known that H=12 m and r=4 m, so the height of point C is 2r=8 m. When the slider reaches point C, the pressure on the track is exactly zero, so at the top point of the circular ring there is mg=mv_C^2/r, giving v_C^2=gr. Thus the equivalent height of the mechanical energy at point C is 2r+v_C^2/(2g)=8+4/2=10 m. In the process from A to C, the initial equivalent height of mechanical energy at point A is H=12 m, so in the rising half-circle from B to C, the energy lost due to friction is equivalent to mg(12-10)=2mg. When the slider continues from C through F back to B, the friction inside the circular ring still does negative work, so the equivalent height h of mechanical energy after leaving the circular ring and entering BD must be less than 10 m. Also, because on the descending half-circle from C to B, at the same height the mechanical energy of the slider is less than that on the rising half-circle from B to C, the speed is smaller, the track's supporting force is also smaller, and the corresponding friction force is smaller; the friction loss on the descending half-circle is less than the 2mg on the rising half-circle. Therefore h is greater than 10-2=8 m. In summary, from only these conditions it can be determined that 8 m<h<10 m; if the problem requires giving a possible value, then 9 m satisfies this range, so h may be 9 m.
